variations.prompt: A class remains on Apex API 66.0, but its query explicitly uses WITH USER_MODE. Must it move to 67.0 for that query to enforce the user's CRUD, FLS, and sharing?

No. Explicit user mode already applies those checks.

title: with sharing is not every security check

with sharing alone does not enforce CRUD and FLS.

whyOthers.text: For system-mode operations, the class sharing declaration still governs record-level sharing behavior.

A system-mode query does not automatically enforce object Read and field-read permissions.

title: A recursion guard that skips work
prompt: Within one transaction, a trigger handles several record chunks. A single static Boolean becomes true after the first invocation and stays true for that transaction. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: The static flag persists across unrelated users' transactions, so one user's save blocks the next user's save.

Later chunks or necessary repeated passes can be skipped entirely.
It automatically resets for every record.

One flag does not track individual records.

title: What Database.Stateful preserves
prompt: A Batch accumulates an instance field total across several execute calls and needs it in finish. What preserves that value between batch transactions?

Database.AllowsCallouts.

variations.prompt: A Batch implements Database.Stateful, but its counter is static Integer total. Is that a reliable combined total across execute transactions?

options.text: Yes. Stateful preserves every static field.

Yes, if the static counter is initialized in the batch constructor.

Initialization does not make later static-field changes persist across execute transactions.

title: A partially failing Batch

No. Batch chunk execution order is not guaranteed.

whyOthers.text: State retention does not guarantee execution order.
A smaller scope changes chunk size, not the documented guarantee about chunk execution order.
The documentation does not promise that.

title: When Queueable fits
prompt: After an appointment save, you need bounded background work, structured class parameters, and a job Id for tracking. Volume and limits are understood. Which mechanism fits?

title: Why use startTest and stopTest?

After Test.stopTest(), when the collected async work has run in the test.
Inside the Queueable constructor, because it runs in the later asynchronous transaction.

title: Named versus External Credentials
prompt: Apex calls an external API. How should you separate endpoint configuration from authentication without putting a password in code?

title: Choose REST or SOAP from the contract

Treat the timeout as proof that the remote transaction rolled back before retrying.
Use a stable idempotency or business key and check for an already completed operation.

whyOthers.text: That prevents recognition of the same operation.

title: Test an external HTTP API
prompt: An Apex unit test must cover a successful HTTP response and a service error without the live API. What should it use?

HttpCalloutMock and Test.setMock with controlled responses.

title: connectedCallback can run again

whyOthers.text: A window listener is attached to a global object and needs explicit cleanup by the component.

title: A rerender loop
prompt: Every renderedCallback assigns new state used by the template, producing a rerender loop. What should you investigate first?

options.text: Reactive-state changes inside renderedCallback; remove the cycle or guard one-time initialization.
Move the same state assignment into Promise.then from every renderedCallback; scheduling it later removes the cycle.

title: @track and Date
prompt: A template uses @track when = new Date(). Code mutates it with when.setDate(...). Why should you not rely on @track to observe that mutation?

title: What cacheable Apex can do

variations.prompt: Save must change records. LWC calls the method imperatively, and caching is unnecessary. Which contract fits?

Only the result.data array.
The Promise returned by calling the imported Apex method imperatively.

variations.prompt: After an imperative Apex update, another component displays the same records through Lightning Data Service. How should LDS be told the records are stale?

Change a local variable; every LDS cache will notice.
Refresh an unrelated Apex @wire and assume this invalidates every LDS record cache.
Call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with the changed record Ids.

whyOthers.text: That is the wrong API and argument type.
Local state does not notify LDS.

title: LMS across separate components
prompt: Two components occupy separate DOM branches in Lightning Experience. An LWC must communicate a selected record Id in a supported container. Which mechanism fits?

title: The Shadow DOM boundary

title: Do all events need bubbles and composed?

options.text: Always use capture; it is LWC's only phase.

whyOthers.text: LWC does not support capture-phase dispatch/listeners.

title: Why Apex wire is not called
prompt: A reactive Apex @wire parameter is undefined. The method and other configuration are valid. What should happen?

options.text: The wire throws a configuration error and never reevaluates when the parameter later receives a value.
The Apex method is not called while that parameter is undefined.
The method receives an empty string.
The method necessarily receives null.

whyOthers.text: An undefined parameter prevents the call for that configuration; a later reactive value can enable it.
undefined is not automatically converted that way.

variations.prompt: In the same Apex @wire configuration, the parameter is explicitly null and the other parameters are set. Does null itself prevent the call?

options.text: Yes. null and undefined behave identically.
Yes. cacheable=true suppresses every call containing a null argument.
No, but wire replaces null with the last non-null parameter value held in the cache.
No. The method is called with null; Apex determines how to handle it.

whyOthers.text: The documentation distinguishes them.
Caching does not change the documented distinction between null and undefined wire parameters.
An explicit null is passed as null; it is not silently replaced by a previous parameter value.

variations.explanation: null is a parameter value, unlike undefined's unavailable configuration.

title: Publish after a successful save
prompt: A Platform Event subscriber immediately reads a record created by the publishing transaction. No event should appear if that transaction rolls back. Which publish behavior fits?

Keep Publish Immediately and call EventBus.publish last in the method; that guarantees commit happens first.

whyOthers.text: It can publish before commit or despite rollback.
The subscriber executes separately.
Being the last method statement is not a transaction commit boundary and does not change Publish Immediately semantics.

variations.prompt: A diagnostic event does not depend on a committed record and should be able to publish even if the transaction later rolls back. Which behavior fits?

options.text: Every mode publishes during rollback.
Use Publish After Commit and check a successful SaveResult to force publication before rollback.
Publish Immediately.
Publish After Commit.

whyOthers.text: After Commit depends on successful completion.
A successful queuing result neither changes the event's publish behavior nor creates a commit.
A rolled-back transaction does not publish its After Commit event.

variations.explanation: It can publish independently of the eventual commit; consumers must not assume the transaction's data is saved.

title: Can you add one to a Replay ID?
prompt: A Pub/Sub API client stores the last processed event's Replay ID. Can it calculate the next Replay ID as previous + 1?

options.text: Yes. Replay IDs always have no gaps.
Yes, for events belonging to one object.
Yes, after decoding the Replay ID into a number; its encoding is the only obstacle.
No. Replay ID is an opaque position; retain the received value for resumption.

whyOthers.text: Consecutive values are not guaranteed.
That does not change their opaque nature.
A decoded representation does not establish a contiguous sequence or make arithmetic a supported continuation strategy.

title: Publisher and subscriber have separate transactions

options.text: Yes, if the publisher and subscriber execute under the same user.
No, because EventBus.publish guarantees retrying the subscriber until every business operation succeeds.
No. The subscriber's separate transaction cannot undo the publisher's earlier commit.
Yes. The event bus automatically rolls back the publisher.

whyOthers.text: A shared user identity does not merge their separate transactions.
The earlier commit remains because transactions are separate, not because EventBus.publish guarantees eventual subscriber success.
There is no such shared transaction.

explanation: Observe subscriber failures and design recovery; asynchronous exchange does not create one shared transaction.

title: Move one corrective commit
prompt: A feature branch contains one independent fix. The release branch needs that fix without all the feature branch's other commits. What fits?

options.text: Run git reset --hard <fix-sha> on release; it copies only that patch and keeps all other release commits.
Cherry-pick the selected commit, resolve any conflicts, and verify the result.
git fetch automatically applies the fix to current files.
git merge feature always transfers only its last commit.

whyOthers.text: Reset moves the branch to that commit and changes its state; it does not apply only the selected commit's patch.
Fetch retrieves objects and refs, not a chosen patch.
Merge integrates histories, not just one selected change.

explanation: Cherry-pick applies a chosen commit's change. It does not guarantee no conflicts or missing dependencies.

title: A token does not replace permissions
prompt: An integration obtains an OAuth access token, but FLS denies a required field read. What should be corrected?

options.text: Review the integration user's minimum required object and field access; the token does not grant those rights.
Request the full OAuth scope; it overrides the integration user's FLS.
Use the JWT bearer flow for the same user; that authentication flow bypasses FLS.
Add the field to the integration user's page layout to grant API Read access.

whyOthers.text: OAuth scopes do not grant field permissions that the authenticated user lacks.
Changing how the same user authenticates does not remove that user's field-access restrictions.
Layout presentation does not grant field-level security for API reads.

explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions. A token is not administrator access.

title: Undo a published ordinary commit
prompt: An ordinary non-merge commit is already on a shared branch and colleagues have fetched it. You need to undo its changes while preserving history. What fits?

options.text: Always use reset --hard and force push without coordination.
git fetch removes the bad commit.
Drop the commit with interactive rebase and force-push; this preserves the already published commit history.
Use git revert and verify the resulting inverse change.

whyOthers.text: That rewrites the shared history the requirement preserves.
Fetch does not undo commits.
Dropping a published commit through rebase rewrites history; revert creates a new inverse commit instead.

title: Why Limits Shape the Architecture
prompt: A team wants to request an increase to every governor limit instead of changing its data processing. Why is that an unreliable design?

options.text: A multitenant platform shares resources; the design must account for limits and measured demand.
Bulkifying Apex removes transaction limits, so only daily API quotas need review.
Queueable gives each job a fresh budget, so total job demand no longer affects org capacity.
A higher org API allocation automatically raises the SOQL-row and CPU limits of each transaction.

whyOthers.text: Bulk processing reduces repeated work but does not exempt a transaction from governor limits.
Separate transaction budgets do not remove shared allocations, scheduling constraints, or downstream capacity.
An org-level API allocation and per-transaction Apex limits govern different resources.

explanation: Limits protect resources shared by multiple customers. Control the amount of work in each transaction rather than assuming every constraint can be removed.

title: An Indexed Query Is Still Slow
prompt: An object contains several million records. A filter on indexed Status__c returns 80% of them. The team says the index must make this query fast. What should you examine?

options.text: Only whether the index exists; that completes the investigation.
Only the batch size, because it changes WHERE selectivity.
Add ORDER BY Status__c; sorting an indexed field always forces the filter to use that index.
Selectivity and actual Query Plan estimates; an index alone does not guarantee a useful plan.

whyOthers.text: The number of matching records and the selected plan also matter.
A processing chunk size does not change the query's data distribution.
Sorting can affect planning but does not guarantee that the optimizer will use the indexed filter.

explanation: The optimizer compares plans using data statistics and estimated cost. An index can be a poor choice when the filter matches most records.

variations.prompt: Query Plan shows a low-cost selective plan, and the query is fast. A debug log shows that almost all CPU time goes to repeatedly scanning large Apex collections. What should you optimize first?

options.text: Rewrite the WHERE clause without further measurements.
The collection-processing algorithm, such as replacing nested searches with Map lookups.
Re-create the same index.
Immediately increase the number of parallel jobs.

whyOthers.text: The measured delay occurs after the query.
The evidence does not identify the query plan as the problem.
That does not reduce CPU work within one transaction.

variations.explanation: When measurements locate the bottleneck in Apex CPU, another index will not fix it.

title: Replace Repeated Searches by Id
prompt: For every Opportunity, the code scans a large Account collection. Both collections are already loaded. How can you reduce comparisons without additional SOQL?

options.text: Add a SOQL query by AccountId inside the outer loop.
Replace List<Account> with Set<Account> but keep the same nested scan.
Build a Map<Id, Account> once and retrieve each Account by o.AccountId.
Move the same double loop into a Queueable.

whyOthers.text: That creates a query per record and risks exceeding limits.
Keeping the nested scan preserves the main search cost.
Moving the code does not reduce the number of comparisons.

explanation: The map avoids a complete Account scan for every Opportunity. This changes the algorithm, not merely where it runs.

title: More Workers Caused More Locks
prompt: Several jobs update different child records of the same heavily used parent. UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW errors increase as jobs are added. What is the best first step?

options.text: Increase batch size because fewer transactions eliminate competition between workers for the parent.
Identify the related records being locked and partition or coordinate work by parent to reduce contention for the same Id.
Double parallelism so that every update gets its lock sooner.
Immediately retry the entire failed batch in every worker without changing how work is partitioned.

whyOthers.text: Larger transactions do not remove the shared parent and can hold locks longer.
More contenders for the same record usually worsen the conflict.
Immediate retries add load while leaving the contested parent and competing workers unchanged.

variations.prompt: Work is partitioned across independent parents. Measurements show no shared lock contention, and available resources and limits allow more load. How should you test whether parallelism improves throughput?

options.text: Always run everything sequentially regardless of the data.
Set the worker count to the largest permitted value and assume that it gives the best throughput.
Add FOR UPDATE to every record read.
Increase workers gradually while measuring throughput, errors, and latency.

whyOthers.text: That can unnecessarily restrict throughput when records are independent.

Unnecessary locks do not accelerate independent work.

variations.explanation: Parallel work can help when operations are independent, but measurements and resource limits determine its useful range.

title: One Owner Holds Most Records
prompt: A service user owns hundreds of thousands of records and is frequently moved between roles used by sharing rules. Why have these changes become expensive?

The main cost must be recalculating object CRUD and FLS, because roles assign those permissions.
The owned-record count is irrelevant because a role change processes only the User record.

whyOthers.text: Changing a user's role is not the same as transferring ownership of all their records.
Roles contribute to record access; profiles and permission assignments supply object and field permissions.
Role and group changes can affect sharing across the user's large collection of owned records.

explanation: Concentrated ownership is not automatically a defect, but changing it can affect a very large set of shares. Evaluate both owner distribution and the stability of the access model.

variations.prompt: A service user owns a large historical dataset, but ownership and roles are stable. The team sees the figure 10,000 and proposes an immediate redistribution without measuring anything. How should you assess it?

options.text: Redistribute immediately because reducing every owner's count below 10,000 always reduces operational risk.
Skip the assessment because historical records never participate in sharing recalculation.
Treat concentration as a risk signal, then measure current operations and the impact of the proposed ownership transfer.
Treat the 10,001st owned record as always prohibited.

whyOthers.text: The transfer itself can create load and access changes; a threshold does not prove that this intervention is safer.
A record's historical business status does not automatically remove it from the sharing model.
This is not a universal hard limit on records per owner.

variations.explanation: A data-skew threshold guides design; it does not prove that a mass transfer is safer now. The transfer itself can cause expensive access recalculation.

title: Finish a Deferred-Sharing Window
prompt: An org has deferred sharing calculations enabled. An administrator suspends sharing-rule calculations, changes participating groups, and selects Resume. What is required for changes accumulated during the pause?

options.text: Nothing; Resume guarantees a full recalculation of accumulated changes.

Check that the sharing rules are active and close the window; active rules prove that stored access is current.
Run a full Recalculate and verify access after it finishes.

whyOthers.text: The documentation requires a separate Recalculate step.
Do not substitute an assumed background schedule for the documented full Recalculate step.
An active configuration does not establish that access affected by accumulated changes has been recalculated.

explanation: Resume restarts processing for new changes. A full recalculation is required for changes accumulated during the pause; otherwise access can remain inconsistent.

variations.prompt: Sharing-rule calculations are suspended. An administrator creates a Manual share. Must that operation wait for Resume along with every other sharing change?

options.text: No; every sharing change created after Suspend bypasses the pause, including new sharing rules.
No. Deferring sharing-rule calculations does not pause every sharing mechanism; manual shares are processed separately.

whyOthers.text: The deferral still covers relevant sharing-rule calculations; the exception for manual shares is not universal.

title: Migrate SECURITY_ENFORCED to API 67
prompt: A class compiled at API 66.0 with WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED. The query fails to compile after the class moves to API 67.0. Which migration should you evaluate?

options.text: Remove every security clause and assume API 67.0 data operations default to system mode.
Keep WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED but move the query into Database.query so the unsupported clause is accepted at API 67.0.
Use WITH USER_MODE and test the resulting access-check behavior.
Keep SECURITY_ENFORCED and assign more permission sets.

whyOthers.text: At API 67.0, data operations default to user mode.
Constructing dynamic SOQL does not restore support for an unsupported security clause.
Permission assignments cannot fix a compilation error.

explanation: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is no longer supported at API 67.0. User mode checks access more broadly, so this is a behavior migration, not just a text replacement.

title: An Omitted Sharing Keyword Depends on API Version
prompt: Two classes omit with, without, and inherited sharing. One uses API 66.0; the other uses API 67.0. Which description of the defaults is accurate?

options.text: Omitting the keyword is equivalent to explicitly declaring inherited sharing in every version and entry point.
At 67.0 the default is with sharing; at 66.0 and earlier an omitted keyword preserves the current sharing context.
In both versions, omitting the keyword always means without sharing.
In both versions, omitting the keyword always means with sharing.

whyOthers.text: An omitted declaration and an explicit inherited-sharing contract are not universally interchangeable; versioned defaults matter.
The default changed at 67.0, and older behavior depends on context.
That is not true for every older calling context.

explanation: The older omitted keyword does not universally mean 'always without sharing.' The calling context and API version matter; an explicit contract makes review easier.

title: Custom Sharing Reasons on Standard Objects
prompt: A team uses Metadata API 68.0 and a supported standard object with a share object and sharing-compatible OWD. Is it still true that custom Apex sharing reasons are available only for custom objects?

options.text: No. API 68.0 adds sharing reasons for supported standard objects; check the object and org requirements.
Yes; this is a permanent platform restriction.
No; every object now has its own share table, including master-detail children.
No; API 68.0 accepts any new RowCause string without defining a supported sharing reason.

whyOthers.text: Current API 68.0 documentation changes that restriction.
Support requires a suitable object and share object.
Custom sharing reasons remain defined metadata with object and version requirements; arbitrary strings do not create them.

explanation: Older articles describe the previous restriction. The new capability does not automatically cover every object, such as a master-detail child without its own share table.

variations.prompt: Project__c is a custom object with its own share table. Programmatic rules A and B grant shares using different custom sharing reasons. You must revoke only access granted by A. Which filter is appropriate?

options.text: Filter only by UserOrGroupId, because shares for the same recipient must come from the same rule.
Filter only by AccessLevel, because the access level uniquely identifies the rule that granted it.
Delete only shares owned by rule A, matching its RowCause and the intended records and recipients.
Delete every Project__Share for those records without checking RowCause.

whyOthers.text: The same recipient can receive independent grants from rules A and B.
Independent rules can grant the same access level; access level does not identify the grant's source.
That can revoke access granted by another rule.

variations.explanation: Separate sharing reasons let code manage its own source of access without removing independent grants.

title: Overlapping Restriction Rules
prompt: An object has two active restriction rules, and one user matches both. The team expects the two record filters to be combined with AND. What should change?

options.text: Nothing; the platform always combines all matching rules with AND.
Nothing; the platform always combines the rules with OR.
Activate the desired rule last, because the most recently activated rule has guaranteed priority.
Design the user criteria so that only one active rule applies to a given user.

whyOthers.text: That behavior is not guaranteed.
That composition is not promised either.
Activation order is not a supported substitute for designing non-overlapping user criteria.

explanation: Salesforce does not validate mutual exclusivity. When two active rules apply to a user, only one is observed; do not rely on AND composition.

title: Recover After Event Retention Expires
prompt: A Pub/Sub client was offline for five days. It has a saved Replay ID, but the required Platform Events are older than the standard 72-hour retention window. Which recovery plan is reliable?

options.text: Subscribe from EARLIEST and assume it includes events that have already expired.
Create a new subscription because unread events are retained indefinitely for every offline client.
Reconcile against a durable source of truth and backfill; replay beyond retention is not guaranteed.
Keep retrying the old Replay ID until the platform is guaranteed to return everything.

whyOthers.text: The earliest available retained event is not the beginning of an unlimited historical archive.
Client absence does not extend the platform's documented event retention window.
There is no such guarantee beyond retention.

explanation: The event bus is not a permanent archive. Long outages require a separate way to recover business state.

variations.prompt: A Pub/Sub client stopped briefly, and its checkpoint is still within available retention. How should it resume after the last processed event?

options.text: Use the saved Replay ID received from the service and handle possible redelivery.
Subscribe from LATEST and assume it also replays everything published during the interruption.
Calculate a new Replay ID from the current time.
Advance the checkpoint before persisting each business result, then resume after that checkpoint.

whyOthers.text: Starting with new events does not recover the retained events missed during the outage.
A Replay ID is not a timestamp that clients can calculate.
A crash can leave the checkpoint ahead of durable processing and cause unfinished work to be skipped.

variations.explanation: Replay can resume a stream within retained history. The consumer must still prevent duplicate business effects.

title: Do Not Treat Replay ID as a Universal Unique Key
prompt: A Pub/Sub Platform Event consumer needs an event identifier for deduplication. Why is replay_id alone insufficient as a universally unique key?

options.text: Pub/Sub guarantees exactly-once business processing, so the consumer needs no deduplication identity.
Replay ID identifies a stream position and can lose uniqueness in certain maintenance scenarios; use event.id and business idempotency.
Republishing the same business operation always reuses its original replay_id.
Replay ID is always unique across every stream and all time.

whyOthers.text: Transport delivery does not guarantee that a business effect is applied exactly once.
A newly published event can represent an already attempted business operation while receiving a different stream position.
The documentation describes exceptions, including some migration scenarios.

explanation: A Platform Event has a separate event.id. Do not assume that this exact field contract also applies to Change Data Capture.

title: A Successful Publish Result Is Not Business Completion
prompt: EventBus.publish returns a successful SaveResult. Can the publisher immediately mark external delivery and business processing as complete?

options.text: No. Successfully queueing publication does not confirm that an external subscriber completed its work.
Yes; SaveResult proves that every subscriber committed successfully.
Yes, with Publish After Commit, because that mode waits for every subscriber before returning success.
Yes; enabling a publish success callback also confirms the external subscriber's business processing.

whyOthers.text: The publisher receives no such guarantee through SaveResult.
Publish After Commit relates publication to the publisher's commit; it does not wait for all subscriber business work.
A publish callback reports publication outcome, not downstream delivery or business completion.

explanation: Publication, delivery, and processing are separate stages. Business completion needs its own acknowledgement or status contract. Publish callbacks can report the final publication result.

title: The Queue Grows Every Day
prompt: After a process moves entirely to Queueable, users no longer wait, but the queue grows every day. What actually changed?

options.text: A growing queue proves the design is healthy because accepted jobs are guaranteed to finish within the user's deadline.
Higher async transaction limits necessarily increased the org's sustained completion rate.
Increasing how often jobs are enqueued will drain the backlog even if their processing rate stays unchanged.
Waiting moved to the queue; compare incoming demand with completion capacity and control or batch the work.

whyOthers.text: Acceptance into a queue does not establish a completion-time guarantee or a sustainable processing rate.
A larger budget for one execution does not establish greater aggregate completion capacity.
More arrivals do not drain existing work when completion capacity is unchanged.

explanation: Async processing does not create unlimited resources or a guaranteed start-time SLA. Monitor queue age, define acceptable delay, and manage demand.

title: QueryLocator Capacity Is Not Transaction Capacity
prompt: A Batch start method returns a QueryLocator covering millions of records. The team proposes loading all related data into every execute call because QueryLocator supports up to 50 million records. What is wrong?

options.text: Database.Stateful moves retained records outside the execute heap budget.
The QueryLocator allowance also permits every SOQL query inside execute to return up to 50 million rows.
The special QueryLocator allowance in start does not remove heap, CPU, or query limits in execute.
QueryLocator automatically splits any nested code into additional transactions.

whyOthers.text: Preserving instance state does not make that state exempt from applicable memory limits.
The special start QueryLocator allowance does not extend to arbitrary queries in execute.
The execute boundary does not automatically subdivide arbitrary logic.

explanation: Every batch scope must fit its own transaction limits. A large total dataset does not mean it can all be processed in one transaction.

title: Use the Sanitized Records
prompt: At API 66.0, this code queries Accounts in system mode. It intends to remove unreadable fields before returning data to the client. Why does it fail to meet that goal?

options.text: stripInaccessible supports write preparation only and cannot sanitize queried records for a read response.
It returns the original rows instead of decision.getRecords().
Returning records to a client requires UPDATABLE rather than READABLE, even for a read-only response.
Nothing is wrong: stripInaccessible mutates the original rows in place before return.

whyOthers.text: AccessType.READABLE can sanitize records for reading; the caller must use the returned records.
READABLE is the relevant field-access check for a read response.
The sanitized records are obtained from SObjectAccessDecision; returning the original list defeats the intended filtering.

explanation: stripInaccessible returns the sanitized records separately. Use those records and also enforce the required record-level access.

title: A Bind Protects a Value, Not a Field Name
prompt: A user-selected sort field is inserted after ORDER BY. WHERE values already use bind variables. What additional protection is needed?

options.text: Allowlist permitted field names and sort directions; value binding does not protect query structure.
Nothing; one bind in WHERE protects the entire SOQL string.
Use String.escapeSingleQuotes(sortField) as the only validation of the field name and sort syntax.
Run the query with WITH USER_MODE, which automatically validates client-supplied ORDER BY syntax against the application's allowed choices.

whyOthers.text: It protects only the corresponding value.
Escaping quotes does not establish that a structural query fragment is a permitted field and direction.
User mode enforces access; it does not define or validate the application's permitted dynamic query structure.

explanation: Field names and keywords are not ordinary bound values. Restrict dynamic structural choices and apply the appropriate access mode separately.

title: OFFSET Cannot Page Through Unlimited History
prompt: A screen must browse tens of thousands of records. It generates SOQL with LIMIT 50 OFFSET page * 50. What has the design missed?

options.text: LIMIT 50 automatically removes the OFFSET limit.
ORDER BY Name removes the 2,000 limit.
Reset OFFSET to zero after reaching 2,000 and deduplicate in the browser; this guarantees eventual access to every record.
SOQL OFFSET is limited to 2,000; this volume needs another continuation strategy.

whyOthers.text: Page size does not remove the maximum offset.
Sorting does not change that limit.
Repeating the same range does not advance beyond it and cannot guarantee traversal of the full dataset.

explanation: Choose a strategy for the use case: query/queryMore for API traversal, a supported-version cursor API, or pagination by a stable key for a UI. OFFSET cannot grow indefinitely.

variations.prompt: A catalog has 300 records and pages of 20. It uses valid OFFSET values and a stable ORDER BY. Records can change between requests. What can you still not promise?

options.text: That ORDER BY can specify an order.
An unchanged snapshot across pages; OFFSET does not create a shared server-side cursor.
That SOQL supports OFFSET at all.
That LIMIT can be combined with OFFSET.

whyOthers.text: ORDER BY controls ordering, but it does not freeze data between requests.
OFFSET is supported within its constraints.
Combining them is supported and commonly needed.

variations.explanation: OFFSET is usable within its limit, but inserted or deleted records can shift page boundaries.

title: What a Green Pull Request Actually Proves
prompt: CI checked only JavaScript formatting. The pull request also changes Apex and metadata. Which evidence is still missing?

options.text: Only that LWC Jest tests pass, because those tests also execute the changed Apex handlers.
Only that the metadata XML is well formed, because this proves that every referenced field and feature exists.
That the metadata deploys and the required Apex behavior passes tests in a suitable org.
Only that an existing org reports 75% coverage, because the percentage proves the changed behavior is correct.

whyOthers.text: LWC Jest tests run JavaScript with appropriate mocks; they do not execute Apex in a Salesforce org.
Valid XML syntax does not prove that the metadata dependencies are present or deployable.
A coverage percentage does not validate the changed deployment or establish correct business outcomes.

explanation: Different parts need appropriate checks, such as static analysis, LWC tests, deployment validation, and Apex tests. One formatter does not validate the whole application.

title: A Clean Org Exposes a Missing Dependency
prompt: An application works in a personal dev org but fails to deploy to a fresh, suitably configured scratch org. A previously hand-created field is missing. What did the check reveal?

options.text: A data-seeding dependency: importing records with the missing field will create its metadata definition.
An untracked metadata dependency; include the required field and configuration in reproducible source.
A temporary deployment-order issue: retrying the same incomplete source will supply the missing definition.
A permission-only issue: granting FLS can substitute for deploying the field definition.

whyOthers.text: Importing business records does not create a missing custom-field definition.
Repeating a deployment cannot supply metadata that is absent from its reproducible source.
Field permissions do not create the field metadata they refer to.

explanation: A clean environment exposes manual changes missing from the project. Required features and licenses must also match the application.

variations.prompt: A project requires an industry feature unavailable in the chosen scratch-org configuration. What should the CI plan do?

options.text: Create a field with the same name and declare the product fully reproduced.
Exclude the product-dependent metadata from CI and treat the remaining green checks as full product validation.
Put the feature's name into the scratch definition and assume this supplies any unavailable product or license.
Use a supported environment and document required features and licenses; this error alone does not prove the code is broken.

whyOthers.text: A matching field name does not replace the industry capability.
Checking only the remaining subset leaves the product integration unverified.
A definition can request supported features; it does not guarantee an unavailable product or entitlement.

variations.explanation: Reproducibility requires a suitable environment. Scratch orgs are useful but do not guarantee access to every product and license.

title: Coverage Does Not Verify the Result
prompt: A test covers every handler line but only checks that no exception occurred. A discount-calculation bug goes unnoticed. What adds useful assurance?

options.text: Assert business outcomes for normal and boundary data, including bulk and negative cases.
Assert only that the result is non-null and treat that as verification of the discount calculation.
Assert only the number of output records and treat matching counts as proof that their discounts are correct.
Replace the discount calculation with a mock returning the expected amount in every test of that calculation.

whyOthers.text: A non-null result can still contain an incorrect discount.
Correct record counts do not establish correct calculated values.
Mocking away the calculation under test prevents those tests from detecting its implementation defect.

explanation: Coverage records executed lines, not correct calculations. Assertions must distinguish the intended result from an incorrect one.

title: Test Access with Restricted Personas
prompt: A new Apex endpoint must return only records and fields available to the caller. All tests currently use very broad access. What additional checks are needed?

options.text: Only a test under a second administrator.
Hide fields on a page layout in the test org.
Check only HTTP 200 and ignore the response body.
Positive and negative cases for restricted users, verifying the actual access mode and returned result.

whyOthers.text: That user can have the same broad permissions and never exercise denial.
Layout visibility is not equivalent to FLS or server-side enforcement.
The test must verify which data is actually returned.

explanation: An administrator can hide access-model defects. Define expected records, fields, and denials; merely using runAs without understanding access mode is insufficient.

title: Do Not Retry an Invalid Payload Forever
prompt: A service returns HTTP 400 because a required country code is absent. The queue retries the identical request every second. What is a better response?

options.text: Retry the unchanged payload with exponential backoff until it succeeds, without correcting the missing country code.
Generate a new business key for every retry.
Record the data error, route it for correction, and retry after the cause changes.
Refresh the OAuth token and retry unchanged, because a missing-field HTTP 400 indicates expired credentials.

whyOthers.text: Backoff controls retry pressure but does not repair a known permanent data-validation error.
That does not repair the payload and can defeat deduplication.
The response identifies invalid request data; replacing credentials does not supply the required country code.

explanation: Not every failure is temporary. Repeating an unchanged invalid request wastes limits and hides the defect; transient failures need a separate retry policy.

title: One Convincing Agent Answer Is Not a Regression Suite
prompt: After an Agentforce action changes, one sample conversation looks convincing. How should you check readiness for the course scenario?

options.text: Use only the same successful wording under an administrator and accept a fluent confirmation as the pass condition.
Run a suite with expected actions and outcomes, including restrictions and invalid requests, and compare runs.
Check only the final response text without verifying the selected action or resulting record changes.
Rely only on the action's unit tests and assume they also prove the agent will select and use it correctly.

whyOthers.text: That narrow case does not exercise varied requests, restricted access, or the actual business effect.
A plausible answer can conceal an incorrect action, unauthorized access, or a missing write.
Action-level tests do not by themselves test the agent's end-to-end decisions and interactions.

explanation: One successful answer cannot establish reliable behavior. Agentforce provides Testing Center, DX, and Testing API options; choose according to the workflow and supported environment.

variations.prompt: A team assumes Agentforce Testing API runs never change data and all related queries are free. What does the current documentation require them to consider?

options.text: Tests automatically roll back absolutely every change.
Testing is supported only in production.
Every Data 360 query inside a test is always free.
Tests can change data; the supported testing environment is a sandbox, and Data 360 queries can consume credits.

whyOthers.text: The documentation warns that tests can change data.
The referenced documentation makes agent testing available in sandboxes.
Related queries can consume Data 360 credits.

variations.explanation: This affects test-data preparation and cost estimates. No Einstein Requests or Flex Credits for the test run itself does not mean every dependent operation is free.

title: Update an Outdated Omni-Channel Lab
prompt: In November 2026, a team writes a new lab exclusively for Standard Omni-Channel and presents it as current configuration. What should they check?

options.text: The move to Enhanced Omni-Channel: Standard retired in Summer '26, so verify examples in the current org.
Nothing; Standard and Enhanced are only names for an unchanged page.
Keep the Standard lab because only newly created orgs must use Enhanced; existing orgs remain Standard indefinitely.
Assume every Standard routing example transfers unchanged and skip validation of Enhanced configuration.

whyOthers.text: The documentation describes retirement and capability differences.
The documented retirement and upgrade are not limited to newly created orgs.
The lab must verify current configuration and behavior rather than assuming complete equivalence.

explanation: The documentation describes automatic org upgrades during the Summer '26 rollout. A lab needs current routing configuration and behavior, not screenshots of an obsolete setup.

title: An Industry Lab Needs a Suitable Org
prompt: A course promises an Automotive Cloud lab in any ordinary Trailhead Playground without checking product availability. What is a reliable plan?

options.text: Deploy exported Automotive object metadata into an ordinary Playground and assume metadata alone supplies the product entitlement.
Assume Salesforce Developer Edition includes every industry license.
Assign Automotive permission sets without first checking whether the org has the required product features.
Verify a suitable Automotive Cloud trial or org, its features and limits, and offer an explicitly separate training model if access is unavailable.

whyOthers.text: Metadata deployment does not by itself provide a licensed industry's features and runtime capabilities.
An ordinary Developer Edition does not guarantee every product.
Permission assignments cannot substitute for required product availability and entitlements.

explanation: An industry product is not installed in every training org. Environment access is part of lab preparation, and a simplified model must be clearly identified.

title: Choose Flow or Apex from Requirements
prompt: A simple update to fields on the triggering record already works in a before-save Flow. The team wants to rewrite it in Apex only for a senior portfolio. What evidence should guide the decision?

options.text: Never use Apex on an object that has a Flow.
Assume Apex must be faster because it is compiled, so no comparable measurement or behavior check is needed.
Requirements, complexity, testability, automation order, and measured demand; the author's desired grade is not a design criterion.
Always rewrite every Flow in Apex.

whyOthers.text: They can coexist, but need a coordinated design.
The implementation mechanism alone does not establish a performance improvement or justify changing a working design.
That is not a universal improvement.

explanation: Choose tools for the problem. Record-triggered automation needs an object-wide view of the transaction lifecycle, not an 'always Flow' or 'always Apex' rule.

title: Do Not Assume a Fixed Cache Lifetime
prompt: An LWC displays a cacheable Apex result. Its business logic assumes the cache always lasts exactly five minutes. What should change?

options.text: Keep the five-minute timer because cacheable=true guarantees every client read reflects the latest server data.
Remove the fixed-TTL assumption and use supported refresh mechanisms when the data is known to be stale.
Hard-code a different number of minutes from an older article.
Set cacheable=false but leave the Apex @wire unchanged.

whyOthers.text: A cacheable read can return cached data; the annotation is not a universal freshness guarantee.
That preserves the same fragile dependency.
Wired Apex requires cacheable=true.

explanation: Client cache duration can change. Business correctness must not depend on an undocumented constant lifetime.

title: Read the Operation's Explicit Access Mode
prompt: An Apex API 67.0 class declares without sharing, but its query explicitly uses WITH USER_MODE. How should you evaluate that query?

options.text: It applies the user's sharing, CRUD, and FLS checks; explicit user mode governs the operation.
without sharing always overrides WITH USER_MODE.
API 67.0 prohibits every without sharing class.
The query checks only FLS and never record access.

whyOthers.text: User mode applies user-access checks to the operation.
There is no such blanket prohibition; the privilege contract must be justified.
User mode also enforces sharing.

explanation: The class declaration alone is not the whole security contract. The operation's access mode and Apex version also matter.

title: Partial Success Needs Per-Record Status
prompt: A handler calls Database.insert(rows, false), then marks the entire batch Synced without reading SaveResult. What information is it losing?

options.text: None; allOrNone=false guarantees that every record succeeds.
Failed rows can be identified only through a caught DmlException, so reading SaveResult is unnecessary.
SaveResult contains only one aggregate batch status, so record-level reconciliation is impossible.
Which records failed and why; each status must correspond to that record's result.

whyOthers.text: It permits partial success; it does not guarantee universal success.
With partial-success DML, per-row SaveResult entries report ordinary row failures without requiring a thrown exception.
The result array contains an outcome for each corresponding input record.

explanation: Partial success is a deliberate contract. Successful rows must not hide failures. Retry appropriate failed records while preserving idempotency.
